House Centipede Pest Control — What They Mean & How to Stop Them

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

House Centipede Pest Control: Why They're in Your Home and How to Get Rid of Them

If you just spotted a house centipede racing across your bathroom floor or clinging to your basement wall, you're probably equal parts horrified and confused. Those long, spindly legs and lightning-fast movement are unsettling, to say the least. But here's what most homeowners in Wichita and across Kansas don't realize: house centipedes aren't invading your home to build nests or eat your food — they're hunting. They're predators, and their presence usually means you have other pests they're feeding on. As a locally owned pest control company serving Kansas families since 1987, Shaw's Pest Control has helped hundreds of homeowners understand what house centipedes really mean — and how to solve the problem at the source. In this guide, we'll explain what these creatures are, why they're showing up, and the most effective approach to house centipede pest control.

What Are House Centipedes and Why Do They Look Like That?

House centipedes (Scutigera coleoptrata) are arthropods with 15 pairs of long, banded legs that give them a creepy, alien-like appearance. Unlike the centipedes you might find outdoors under rocks or logs, house centipedes have adapted to living inside human structures. They're usually yellowish-gray with three dark stripes running lengthwise down their bodies, and they can grow up to 1.5 inches long — though their legs make them look much larger.

Despite their alarming looks, house centipedes are actually beneficial predators. They feed on spiders, silverfish, cockroaches, bed bugs, termites, and other household pests. They're nocturnal hunters, which is why you typically see them darting away when you flip on a light at night. They don't damage property, contaminate food, or pose a significant health threat to humans. While they can bite if handled roughly, it's rare and usually no worse than a minor bee sting.

That said, most people don't want to share their living space with multi-legged predators — no matter how "beneficial" they are. And the real issue is this: if you're seeing house centipedes regularly, it's a strong indicator that you have an underlying pest problem feeding them.

Why You're Seeing House Centipedes in Your Home

House centipedes don't show up randomly. They're attracted to two things: moisture and prey. If your home provides both, you're creating the perfect habitat.

Common moisture sources include damp basements, crawl spaces, bathrooms, laundry rooms, and areas with poor ventilation or plumbing leaks. House centipedes need humid environments to survive, so they gravitate toward these spots. But moisture alone won't sustain them — they need food, and that means other pests.

If you're seeing house centipedes regularly, ask yourself: have you noticed silverfish in your bathroom? Small spiders in the corners? Occasional cockroaches? These are the prey species that keep centipedes coming back. You might not see the other pests often because the centipedes are actively hunting them, but they're there.

This is why effective house centipede pest control isn't about killing centipedes — it's about eliminating the conditions and prey that attract them. At Shaw's Pest Control, our Master Tech Certified technicians focus on integrated pest management that addresses the root cause. That means identifying moisture issues, sealing entry points, and treating for the pests that centipedes feed on. When you remove the food source, the centipedes leave on their own. For comprehensive protection, we offer tailored pest control in Wichita that targets the full spectrum of household invaders.

How to Get Rid of House Centipedes (and Keep Them Out)

Getting rid of house centipedes requires a two-pronged approach: habitat modification and source pest elimination.

Step 1: Reduce moisture. Use dehumidifiers in basements and crawl spaces, fix leaky pipes, improve ventilation in bathrooms, and ensure gutters and downspouts direct water away from your foundation. Reducing indoor humidity below 60% makes your home far less hospitable to centipedes.

Step 2: Eliminate their food source. This is the critical step. If you have silverfish, spiders, or cockroaches, you need professional pest control to eliminate them. Treating just the centipedes won't work — new ones will keep coming as long as prey is available. A thorough inspection and targeted treatment plan can break the cycle.

Step 3: Seal entry points. Centipedes enter through cracks in foundations, gaps around pipes, worn weather stripping, and basement windows. Sealing these access points reduces the likelihood of new centipedes entering your home.

Step 4: Remove harborage sites. Declutter basements, remove cardboard boxes stored on damp floors, and clear debris from around your home's exterior. These areas provide hiding spots for both centipedes and their prey.

DIY approaches like sticky traps or insecticide sprays might catch a few centipedes, but they won't address the underlying issue. Professional pest control is the most reliable way to eliminate the problem for good.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are house centipedes dangerous?

No, house centipedes are not dangerous. They can bite if provoked or handled, but bites are rare and cause only minor, localized pain similar to a bee sting. They don't carry diseases or cause structural damage. Their presence is more of an indicator of other pest activity than a direct threat.

Why do I keep seeing house centipedes in my bathroom?

Bathrooms provide the moisture house centipedes need to survive, and they often harbor prey like silverfish and drain flies. If you're seeing centipedes repeatedly in your bathroom, it's a sign of both high humidity and a food source. Improving ventilation and treating for other pests will help eliminate them.

Do house centipedes mean I have a dirty home?

Not at all. House centipedes are attracted to moisture and prey, not cleanliness. Even well-maintained homes can have centipede issues if there's a hidden moisture problem or an unnoticed pest population. It's about environment and access, not hygiene.

How do I get rid of house centipedes naturally?

Reducing moisture is the most effective natural method. Use dehumidifiers, fix leaks, and improve airflow. You can also seal cracks and remove clutter to eliminate hiding spots. However, if centipedes persist, it usually means there's a prey population you'll need professional help to eliminate.

Will house centipedes go away on their own?

House centipedes will leave if their food source disappears and moisture levels drop. But without intervention, they're likely to stay as long as conditions remain favorable. Addressing the root cause — moisture and prey pests — is the only reliable way to make them go away permanently.

What's the best pest control for house centipedes?

The best house centipede pest control targets the pests they feed on, not just the centipedes themselves. A professional inspection can identify moisture issues, entry points, and prey species. Treating the whole problem with an integrated approach is far more effective than spot treatments or DIY sprays.
